module_title: Foundation Model Customization, Evaluation and Bedrock Applications
review_basis: Visually inspected original numbered WebP slides 01, 02 and 03 individually in source order via GitHub image content; checked visible labels, stages, arrows, examples, AWS service references and bottom callouts. Each scene rewritten to teach the corresponding original image in visual reading order.

scenes.title: Fine-tuning a model in Amazon Bedrock
scenes.narration: Look at the title: fine-tuning a model in Amazon Bedrock. The diagram has two phases, training on the left and inference on the right. Start with the green Amazon S3 bucket. It holds curated training examples, such as a customer request paired with the response style or format we want. The format must match the requirements of the selected model. Now follow the blue arrow to the purple Bedrock model customization job. The job combines those S3 examples with a supported base foundation model. Notice the IAM service role underneath: Bedrock needs permission to read the training data, otherwise the job cannot begin. The next panel shows the customized model artifact. Fine-tuning updates model weights, which are the learned parameters controlling its behavior. So this is more than simply changing one prompt. Continue right to the evaluation card. Held-out examples are separate test cases the model did not train on; we use them to check whether tone, format and quality really improved. Finally, the application uses the customized model through a supported deployment option. Read the decision cue at the bottom: fine-tuning is for changing stable behavior or style. If the main requirement is current company facts, a retrieval approach such as a Bedrock Knowledge Base is more appropriate. The support-response example illustrates why: learn a consistent tone, but retrieve an updated policy rather than memorizing it. The supported model, AWS Region, pricing and deployment method must be checked before choosing this design.

scenes.title: Instruction-based fine-tuning
scenes.narration: This slide turns fine-tuning into a six-step example. Begin in box one, the labeled training dataset. Read the first row: 'I cannot sign in' is labeled 'Account access.' The second ticket, 'My invoice is incorrect,' is Billing. App crashes map to Technical issue, while changing a plan maps to Account management. The labels are desired answers, so this is supervised learning. Just below, the separate evaluation set includes 'I was overcharged' with Billing and 'How do I reset my password?' with Account access. These examples test generalization without letting the model simply memorize the training rows. At step two, store both datasets in Amazon S3. Step three selects a supported pretrained foundation model. Follow the yellow arrows down to step four: a fine-tuning job takes that model and the labeled examples to update its behavior. Step five shows the resulting customized model in purple. Now look at step six on the far right. A brand-new ticket says 'I cannot reset my password.' The model returns Account access. That is inference: applying what was learned to a new input. Along the bottom, the dataset format card makes an important distinction. The input is an instruction, such as 'Classify this ticket,' while the desired completion is the label, 'Account access.' The selected model determines the exact allowed dataset schema. Ask yourself: if we trained and evaluated on the very same ticket rows, could the evaluation score be misleading? Yes, because memorization would look like real understanding. That is why the held-out set matters.

scenes.title: Continued pre-training
scenes.narration: The heading is continued pre-training, which is different from the instruction tuning on the previous slide. Follow the four numbered panels from left to right. First is the domain text corpus. The pictured books are Engineering Manuals, Technical Guides, Standards and Terminology; these documents are stored as unlabeled text in Amazon S3. Unlabeled means we do not manually attach a correct answer to every passage. Second, the supported base foundation model goes into an Amazon Bedrock customization job. The text beside the arrow says the original language-model objective continues: next-token prediction, learning which text is likely to follow previous text. Third, the result is a domain-adapted model with updated weights, represented by the larger purple brain. That model may understand specialized vocabulary better, but it is not automatically guaranteed to answer every engineering question correctly. Fourth, the evaluation clipboard lists domain question answering, document summarization, classification and information extraction. These are example tasks to test with separate held-out data, not automatic promises of success. Look at the comparison at the bottom left. Instruction tuning uses manually created instruction and desired-answer pairs, while continued pre-training uses raw domain text without those answer labels. The engineering-documentation example underneath shows design guides, API references, specifications and internal documents. If your goal is to teach an assistant a consistent response format, choose instruction tuning when supported. If you need to adapt language understanding to a large specialist corpus, continued pre-training may fit, subject to model support and evaluation. And if you simply need the latest manual version, retrieve the current document rather than assuming updated model weights contain it.
